extracted.intended_audience: scholars and advanced students of classical mechanics / history of physics (readers of Newton's Principia)
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and restate the substantive propositions, corollaries, and laws given in this excerpt of Newton's Principia (classical-mechanics theorems about attraction, refraction-like trajectory laws, and motion under resistance). Suitable for readers analysing Newton's results or applying them to problems in gravitation and motion with resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum of annular attractions proportional to area×AP
rubrics_metrics.description: The force by which a thin annulus of a circle (center A, interval AD) attracts a particle P toward A is proportional to the product of certain segment lengths (equivalently the area FKkf times AP), and consequently the sum of the attractions of all such annuli in the circle is proportional to the total area AHIKL multiplied by AP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton computes the contribution of a single annulus (PE×Ff & AP×FK ÷ PE conjunctim, i.e. Ff×AP×FK) and sums over annuli; the result used to derive corollaries for particular distance-laws (e.g. inverse-square). (Q.E.D. in text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse-square point-force corollary (Corol. 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If point-forces decrease in the duplicate (square) ratio of distances (i.e. force ∝ 1/d^2), then the area AHIKL equals {1/PA} - {1/PH}, and the attraction of P into the circle is given by the corresponding expression (reduces to a simple reciprocal-distance form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a specialization of the annulus-sum result to the 1/d^2 law; Newton gives the explicit algebraic form for area and the resulting attraction (useful to derive the familiar inverse-square central force consequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: General inverse-power corollary (Corol. 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the point-forces vary reciprocally as any power D^n of distance (force ∝ 1/D^n), then the summed area AHIKL is proportional to {1/PA^(n-1)} - {1/PH^(n-1)}, and the attraction of P into the circle is expressible in terms of PA and PH with exponents shifted accordingly (involving PA^(n-2) etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton provides the general algebraic forms for arbitrary integer exponent n>0; these general formulae reduce to the inverse-square case when n=2 and are used to consider limiting cases (n→...).

rubrics_metrics.name: Planar (infinite-diameter) limit of inverse-power law (Corol. 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the circle's diameter is increased to infinity and n>1, the attraction of P toward the whole (now nearly planar) distribution becomes reciprocally proportional to PA^(n-2) because the other term vanishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives the limiting law for attraction by an infinite plane or very large disk when the elemental forces fall off as 1/d^n; used later for analyzing semi-infinite solids and slabs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attraction on axis of a solid via section-area (Prop. XCI)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a solid of revolution (solid ADEFG) and a particle P on its axis AB, cut the solid by circles perpendicular to the axis; the attraction of P by the solid is proportional to the area LABI generated (i.e. integrate the contributions of circular sections to obtain a corresponding plane area).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: for each circular section take the length FK (Proposition XC) proportional to attraction of that circular section; then the total attraction equals the area LABI (Q.E.D.). This method yields closed forms for cylinders, spheres, etc., by evaluating the corresponding area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cylinder attraction with inverse-square element forces (Corol. 1 to Prop. XCI)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a cylinder (parallelogram ADEB revolved about axis AB) whose constituent centripetal forces at each point vary inversely as the square of the distance from the point, the attraction on a particle P on the axis is proportional to AB - PE + PD (i.e. can be expressed as simple linear combinations of axial segments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton constructs the appropriate ordinates FK and shows how the area LABI reduces to a combination of rectangular areas, giving the algebraic form for the axial attraction of a finite cylinder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attraction of exterior point by spherical shell/spheroid (Corol. 2 & 3 to Prop. XCI)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a spheroid (or sphere) the attraction exerted on an external particle P on the axis can be expressed by algebraic combinations of sphere/spheroid dimensions (Newton gives a formula involving AS, CS, PS, and sectional arc lengths); moreover, if a particle lies inside a homogeneous sphere, the attraction is proportional to its distance from the center (i.e. inside a uniform sphere the force grows linearly with radial distance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary 3 states the classic result: inside a homogeneous sphere the net attraction is as the distance from the center (used to show simple harmonic-like behaviour for interior points). Corollary 2 gives the exterior axial attraction for spheroids in explicit algebraic form; Newton indicates the same method applies to spherical segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse problem: deduce elemental-force law from measured attraction (Prop. XCII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a body with unknown distribution of elemental centripetal forces, one may form a concentric regular figure (sphere or cylinder) whose attraction law matches the observed attraction; by conducting experiments measuring attraction at various distances, the law of attraction of the whole determines the decrement (distribution) of elemental forces of the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton outlines the method: choose a convenient regular figure, measure attraction vs distance, and from the observed law reconstruct the elemental force-decrement law (uses Propositions LXXX–LXXXI and XCI as foundation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attraction of semi-infinite solids with element-force ∝ 1/d^n (Prop. XCIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a solid that is planar on one side and infinite elsewhere, composed of equal mutually attracting particles whose forces decrease as a power of distance higher than quadratic (index n>2), the net attraction of the solid on a particle located near the planar face decreases with distance from the plane in the ratio of a power with exponent (n - 3). In other words, the solid's attractive force ∝ 1/(distance)^(n-3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton proves by slicing the solid into parallel planes and integrating contributions: the plane contributions are proportional to CH^(n-2) reciprocals, and summing (area methods) yields overall decay as CG^(n-3). Special cases and corollaries consider slabs between two parallel infinite planes and the case of internal points; he also notes exceptions when the elemental exponent equals 3 (n=3) where the argument fails due to divergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of sines for trajectory refraction between similar media (Prop. XCIV)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two similar media occupy parallel slab regions and a particle traverses the intervening space being attracted (or impulsed) perpendicularly toward the nearer medium with equal attraction at equal distances, then the sine of the angle of incidence onto one plane is to the sine of the angle of emergence from the other plane in a given (fixed) ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton proves by decomposing motion into perpendicular and parallel components and considering limiting parabolic arcs for uniform perpendicular attraction. This is the mechanical analogue of Snell's law: sine ratios of incident and emergent angles are preserved according to the given ratio of perpendicular actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Velocity ratio equals sine ratio (Prop. XCV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the same assumptions as the preceding proposition, the particle's velocity immediately before incidence is to its velocity immediately after emergence as the sine of emergence is to the sine of incidence (i.e., v_before : v_after = sin_emergent : sin_incident).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton decomposes motion into perpendicular and parallel components and uses equal-times equal-parallel displacements to relate lengths of arcs and hence sines to velocities (Q.E.D.). This connects geometric sine ratios with actual speed changes across the medium interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection law: equal incident and reflected angles (Prop. XCVI)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the particle's speed before incidence is greater than after, then by appropriate inclination of the incident line the particle will be reflected and the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence (i.e., specular reflection law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton constructs the limit of many thin parallel planes (parabolic arcs) and shows that as plane spacing → 0 the emergent direction coincides with a reflection with equal incident and reflected angles. He draws the analogy to optical reflection and refraction (Snell, Descartes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of focusing surface given sine-ratio law (Prop. XCVII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a source point A and a target point B and a prescribed ratio between sine of incidence and sine of emergence at each surface point, one can determine a curve CDE whose revolution about AB gives a surface that will focus all particles emitted from A to B (by enforcing at each point the incremental ratio of path segments AD and DB to match the sine ratio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton provides a differential-geometric construction: selecting an arbitrary point C on axis AB, prescribing increments CM and CN on AC and BC in the given ratio, then drawing the circle with centers A and B and finding its intersection D gives a tangent point to the desired curve; varying C traces the full curve. Corollaries include the limiting cases that reproduce Descartes' optical surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Given first attracting surface, construct second to focus to B (Prop. XCVIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an initial axis AB and an attracting surface CD through which particles from A pass, one can construct a second attracting surface EF (by a geometric construction involving proportional segments and circles) so that particles after passing CD will be refracted by EF and converge to B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton prescribes detailed proportional constructions: extend AB, choose proportional segments, draw circles and parallels to obtain point F; revolving EF about AB gives the required surface. He notes the method generalizes to multiple surfaces and that spherical figures are most practical for optics (Scholium).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion with resistance ∝ velocity: loss ∝ distance (Prop. I, Liber II)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a body's resistance from the medium is proportional to its velocity, then the motion lost by the body from resistance is proportional to the distance traversed (i.e., the decrement in 'motion' accumulates proportionally to path length).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton reasons that if loss per time is proportional to instantaneous velocity (the 'motion' lost each infinitesimal time ∝ v), then integrating over time gives total loss ∝ total distance traveled (Q.E.D.). This yields corollaries about attainable distances in infinite time when gravity is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Velocities form a geometric progression under linear resistance (Prop. II)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a body subject to resistance proportional to velocity and moved by a single internal or applied force through a homogeneous medium, the velocities at the beginnings of equal time intervals are in geometric progression; the distances described in each equal time are proportional to those velocities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton proves by discretizing time into equal parts and letting the resistance impulse per part be proportional to the velocity at the part's start; passing to the continuous limit yields continuously proportional (geometric) velocities. He provides a hyperbola-area representation linking time and velocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projectile motion with linear resistance: curve determined by hyperbola construction (Prop. IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a projectile acted on by gravity and medium resistance proportional to velocity, the trajectory is a specific curve (constructed via a hyperbola with appropriate parameters); the tangents to that curve give instantaneous velocities, and the curve's latus rectum is linked to the ratio of gravity to resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton gives a construction using a hyperbola GTBS, parallelogram DGKC, and proportional relations DC:CP etc.; the resulting parametric curve DraF describes the projectile's path. Corollaries explain how to deduce resistance from observed landing points and how the latus rectum changes with resistance relative to gravity (practical method to infer resistance laws from experiments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance ∝ velocity is a mathematical idealization; real media often quadratic
rubrics_metrics.description: Newton remarks that the hypothesis of resistance proportional to velocity is primarily mathematical and holds approximately only for media where bodies move very slowly; in 'perfect' media resistance is proportional to the square of velocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He explains the physical reasoning: faster bodies impart more motion to the medium in less time (so a quadratic dependence arises when considering transmitted motion per unit time) and indicates that subsequent propositions treat quadratic resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadratic resistance: velocities in inverse geometric progression and equal distances per equal times (Prop. V)
rubrics_metrics.description: If resistance varies as the square of velocity and a body's motion is driven by a single internal force, then taking equal time intervals in geometric progression from small to large, the velocities at the beginnings of those times are in inverse geometric progression, and the distances described in each interval are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton demonstrates by constructing perpendiculars and a hyperbola BklmG; squares of the perpendiculars correspond to velocity-differences; from this the similarity of the progression of squares and that of their differences yields the stated behaviour (useful for analyzing motion in common fluids at higher speeds).
